The Hardyhead silverside Atherinomorus lacunosus is a relatively small-bodied atherinid that attains a maximum recorded total length of 25 centimeters [Li = 25 centimeters], a size that places it among the mid-range members of its genus in tropical Indo-Pacific waters. Field surveys conducted across the Great Barrier Reef indicate that individuals typically reach this asymptotic length within two to three years of age, with growth rates that are strongly modulated by seasonal fluctuations in prey availability and local water temperature. During the early pelagic larval phase, newly hatched individuals emerge from demersal eggs with a minute wet weight at birth of just 0.0028 grams [Wwb = 0.0028 grams], reflecting the limited yolk reserves provisioned within the egg capsule. This extraordinarily low initial mass means that the larvae must commence exogenous feeding almost immediately after the completion of yolk-sac resorption to avoid starvation mortality. The transition from lecithotrophic to exotrophic nutrition represents a critical bottleneck, with first-feeding success rates often determining overall cohort strength in this species.

Reproductive maturation in Atherinomorus lacunosus is attained at a modest body size, with individuals reaching total length at puberty of 9 centimeters [Lp = 9 centimeters], a threshold that corresponds to the onset of active gametogenesis and the first appearance of vitellogenic oocytes in females. Field studies conducted in shallow seagrass habitats of the Philippines have demonstrated that the wet weight at puberty is approximately 7.9 grams [Wwp = approximately 7.9 grams], a body mass that represents roughly four percent of the ultimate wet weight documented for fully grown adults. This early maturation strategy, typical of many tropical atherinids, allows individuals to begin contributing to the next generation before they have completed somatic growth, thereby maximizing lifetime reproductive output in an environment where adult mortality is high due to predation by piscivorous fishes and seabirds. The relatively low weight at puberty also suggests that the species invests minimally in somatic reserves before initiating reproduction, a pattern consistent with an opportunistic life-history strategy adapted to variable coastal environments.

Adults of Atherinomorus lacunosus achieve a maximum wet weight of 198.5 grams [Wwi = 198.5 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions applied to the species' asymptotic length. This ultimate wet weight is among the highest recorded for atherinids of comparable body length, reflecting a relatively robust body shape and the species' tendency to accumulate lipid reserves in mesenteric fat deposits during periods of high prey abundance. Comparative analyses with congeneric species such as Atherinomorus endrachtensis indicate that Hardyhead silverside exhibits a slightly heavier body condition at equivalent lengths, a difference that may be linked to its preferential occupation of nutrient-rich estuarine and coastal lagoon habitats rather than exposed reef flats. The asymptotic mass also shows notable geographic variation, with individuals from higher-latitude populations off the coast of southern Japan attaining slightly lower ultimate weights, suggesting a latitudinal gradient in growth performance that warrants further investigation.

Longevity records for Atherinomorus lacunosus, compiled from mark-recapture studies in the Gulf of Aqaba, indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 4 years [am = approximately 4 years] under the stable thermal conditions of the Red Sea, where mean annual water temperature remains near 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This lifespan is comparatively short for a fish of its ultimate body size, aligning with the general pattern observed among tropical atherinids that exhibit rapid growth, early maturation, and high natural mortality rates. Tagging data further reveal that most individuals in wild populations do not survive beyond their third year, with senescence-related declines in condition and increased susceptibility to parasites becoming particularly evident during the fourth year of life. The relatively brief lifespan constrains the total number of spawning seasons available to each individual, reinforcing the selective advantage of early maturation and high fecundity per reproductive event as compensatory life-history traits in this species.

Fecundity estimates for Atherinomorus lacunosus, based on gravimetric analysis of mature ovaries, indicate that females produce between 1,200 and 3,800 eggs per spawning event, with clutch size positively correlated with female body length. Reproductive activity is strongly seasonal in most parts of the species' range, with spawning occurring primarily during the austral summer months when water temperatures exceed 24 °C. In the thermally stable environment of the northern Red Sea at 25 °C [T = 25 °C], however, reproduction appears to occur year-round, with individual females capable of producing a new clutch every 14 to 18 days during the peak of the breeding season. The combination of relatively large clutch sizes and continuous spawning activity allows populations of this species to sustain high densities even in the face of substantial predation pressure on eggs and early larvae. Field observations of spawning behavior confirm that this species is a broadcast spawner, releasing pelagic eggs into the water column where fertilization occurs externally and the developing embryos drift with prevailing currents.
